page.overview: The School Committee is a body of the school district, not of the town: five members elected town-wide to three-year terms, with general charge of the public schools under Massachusetts General Laws Chapter 71, Section 37. Its page is on the district’s site, which is why it is not on the town’s list of boards.

watch_next: School committee vote on the business administrator hire, expected next Wednesday
Town finance committee meeting the next night, where audit funding is on the agenda

what_happened.line: The school committee will vote next week on hiring a school business administrator, after publicly interviewing a candidate tonight.
The school department will ask the town finance committee to fund a financial and process audit of the school business office from the town's reserve rather than the school budget.
The committee ratified a new three-year contract for cafeteria workers.
Votes on committee operating protocols and this year's goals, including the Turkey Hill Elementary MSBA process, were pushed to next week.
The chair said override funding approved at the recent special town meeting is already being used to reduce second-grade class sizes.

why_it_matters: The business administrator runs school finance day to day, and the committee itself controls this hire and expects to decide it next week.
The proposed audit's funding source determines whose budget absorbs the cost, and it goes to the town finance committee for a decision, not the school committee.
The Turkey Hill Elementary MSBA process is an early procedural step that can lead toward a future building project and a town vote.

ours.headline: The school committee will hire its own next business administrator, deciding by vote next week after tonight's public interview.

watch_next: Special town meeting vote on warrant article 3 (citizens' petition, middle school sports/transportation) and an amount as heard additional state aid appropriation
Warrant article 2, expected to be passed over by its sponsor at town meeting

what_happened.line: Committee voted to restore a second-grade teacher and fund literacy support plus athletic transportation, rather than an outside audit or a second BCBA.
Committee voted to commit any citizens'-petition warrant article 3 funds, if appropriated at special town meeting, to restoring middle school sports.
Committee decided to hold Ignite tutoring at 36 grant-funded seats rather than expand, freeing money for the other scenarios.
Committee will refund transportation donations already collected from boosters and return that decision to the booster clubs.
The private-transportation waiver form will be dropped from final forms if the funding article passes at town meeting.

why_it_matters: The vote decides whether second-grade class sizes shrink and middle/high school literacy support expands, funded from additional state aid the town has not yet appropriated at special town meeting.
Whether middle school sports return depends on a citizens' petition warrant article at that same town meeting, not on this vote alone.
Families who paid privately for athletic transportation, or donated to boosters for it, may see refunds and a change to the waiver paperwork if the article passes.

ours.headline: The committee voted to restore a second-grade teacher and literacy funding over an audit or a second BCBA.

watch_next: The September 3rd special town meeting vote on the school committee's warrant article
The tabled FY26 budget update item, expected at a future meeting

what_happened.line: The committee voted to submit its own warrant article asking the September 3rd special town meeting for the full additional state education aid, rather than relying on a separate citizen petition.
The committee chose to amend and adopt the original petition language as its own article so only one request goes to town meeting.
The committee voted unanimously to ratify a new custodians union (AFSCME Council 93) contract.
The committee accepted several FY26 line item transfers covering overages in maintenance, custodial, transportation, guidance and high school administration salaries.
A further FY26 budget update was tabled rather than voted on.

why_it_matters: Residents will be asked at the September 3rd special town meeting to decide how much of the additional FY27 state aid goes to the schools versus other town needs.
The new custodians' union contract sets pay and terms for school custodial staff and factors into future budgets.
The tabled FY26 budget update means the year's final school spending picture is not yet settled.

ours.headline: The school committee voted to submit its own warrant article demanding the full extra state aid for the September 3rd special town meeting.

watch_next: July 29th meeting: custodial union MOU return
November special town meeting: warrant article for additional FY27 school funding

what_happened.line: The committee approved a spending plan funding reading specialists, an expanded assistant principal role, tutoring seats, and a music teacher increase.
The committee voted on a warrant article for an additional sum for the FY27 school budget, to go to the Select Board and a November special town meeting; the roll call outcome was not fully audible.
The warrant article vote was tabled once, then taken back up after extended, heated debate over pushing for an earlier special town meeting instead of the town manager's proposed November timeline.
A custodial union memorandum of understanding was not voted because the union had not yet reviewed it; it is expected back around July 29th.

why_it_matters: If the warrant article advances, residents at a November special town meeting will be asked to add funding to the already-voted FY27 school budget, drawn from new state education receipts rather than local taxes.

The spending plan touches reading support at two elementary schools, a high school administrative position, online tutoring capacity, and music staffing -- some already committed from health-insurance savings regardless of the warrant article's outcome.
Whether the special town meeting happens in November or sooner determines how quickly any new positions or services could actually start.

ours.headline: The committee approved a spending plan and voted to send a warrant article to the Select Board for extra FY27 school funding.

what_happened.line: The committee voted unanimously to ask the select board for a special town meeting to redirect state aid to schools.
A curriculum report accepted by the committee described zero reading interventionists left at two elementary schools.
Grades 3 and 4 will drop departmentalized teaching next year, moving to one teacher per class instead of rotating teams.
The personnel report, accepted with one abstention, listed numerous staff departures attributed to budget uncertainty.
Four routine line-item transfers passed unanimously, including shifting unspent athletic transportation funds to cover an athletic fees overage.

why_it_matters: A special town meeting request means residents may be asked to vote again on directing state aid into the school budget.

ours.headline: The committee voted unanimously to ask the select board for a special town meeting to redirect state aid into the school budget.

watch_next: Next School Committee meeting: discussion of district finances and whether to pursue another override or funding request
A public budget check before June 30, and action on the deferred line-item transfers

what_happened.line: After the override's defeat, the committee agreed to take up another override or funding request at its next meeting.
Line-item transfers were deferred to the following meeting, with a public budget check planned before June 30.
A proposed physical education credit or waiver for varsity athletes was tabled after two members were absent; the committee will gather information from peer districts first.
The committee voted unanimously to accept a Turkey Hill PTO donation and, later, the facilities and grounds report citing maintenance-contract savings.

The committee also took up FY27 school handbooks and authorizing the superintendent to negotiate a fifth-grade band stipend with the union, but the recording does not make the vote outcome on either audible.

why_it_matters: Another override vote or funding request may come back to residents, following the defeat of the prior one.
The deferred line-item transfers and the pre-June-30 budget check affect how the current fiscal year's school budget closes out.
The tabled PE credit/waiver would change graduation or scheduling requirements for varsity athletes if it comes back for a vote.

ours.headline: After the override's defeat, the committee agreed to weigh another override or funding request at its next meeting.

watch_next: The superintendent's report back on fifth-grade bus-release community feedback
Any future override vote or the community task force's recommendations

what_happened.line: After the override failed, the committee leaned toward implementing a balanced budget built on cuts to class sizes, interventionists, middle school sports and transportation, and high school world language, rather than returning to voters right away.
The committee elected Laura as chair and Tony as vice chair for 2026-2027, with Mandy Gilman named secretary pending her acceptance.
The fifth-grade bus-release procedure was tabled so the superintendent can gather community feedback before any change.
The committee adopted revised policies on cash handling, student data privacy, medication administration, and advertising in schools.
The committee accepted a composite evaluation of the superintendent's first year.

why_it_matters: The override's failure is now translating into specific reductions -- class sizes, interventionist staffing, middle school sports and transportation, and a high school language program -- while the committee weighs a community task force before deciding whether to ask voters again.
The new cash-handling policy sets a cap on cash accepted per school transaction, which came up directly in connection with how prom tickets can be sold going forward.

Families with fourth- and fifth-graders should watch for the superintendent's community feedback process on bus release, since it is being handled as an administrative procedure rather than a committee policy vote.

ours.headline: Override failed; committee accepts a balanced-budget of cuts and eyes another override attempt next year

what_happened.line: Committee heard roughly 90 minutes of testimony on an appeal over a disputed student-council election and took no vote, reserving a written decision.
Members approved a batch of year-end line-item transfers, including moves among substitute-teacher lines and a special education paraprofessional account.
Committee voted to authorize applying for a federal literacy grant, capped at an amount as heard, and for FY27 DESE entitlement grants.
Discussion of loosening the fifth-grade school-bus release consent rule was deferred until the superintendent returns and new legal counsel weighs in.
Committee waived second reading on four policies covering cash handling, student data privacy, medication administration, and school advertising.

why_it_matters: The written decision on the election appeal will set how the district resolves nomination-signature disputes in student government going forward.
Year-end transfers show which school programs, including substitute teaching and special education paraprofessional support, ran short of their budgeted lines.
Any change to fifth-grade bus-release rules affects how parents authorize after-school pickup, and now waits on new legal review before moving forward.

ours.headline: Committee heard a 90-minute appeal over a disputed student-council election signature count, took no vote

watch_next: Superintendent evaluation rubric scores due around May 13, with compilation and discussion at the May 20 meeting
A future agenda item on an extended day program fee increase

what_happened.line: The superintendent and chair urged residents to approach the coming override vote and town meeting collaboratively, calling this year's budget process unusually transparent.
The committee voted to submit two Prism grant applications and a Farm to Table grant to bring in state funding for staff training and curriculum.
A dispute over a scholarship trust fund's EIN with the town's Trust Commission was sent to legal counsel rather than resolved tonight.
First readings were waived on four policies, including student data privacy and security rules that address AI use.
Negotiating teams were assigned for the custodians' and cafeteria workers' union contracts, and a fee increase for the extended day program was pushed to a future agenda.

why_it_matters: The override and town meeting the superintendent referenced would set the tax bill residents vote on, and the meeting framed this year's budget process as more transparent than past years.

ours.headline: Schools urged town unity ahead of the override vote; routine grants and policy readings were approved

watch_next: Business manager's revolving-fund and quarterly budget report, expected at the next meeting (April 15)
Contract negotiations, set to begin the following week with experienced and new members paired up

what_happened.line: The committee voted to continue charging the student bus fee for another year, despite members calling it unfair, citing the district's financial situation.
Members voted to end the district-run Lunenburg lifelong learning program effective June 1, citing minimal revenue and reliance on volunteers or a pass-through vendor.
The committee authorized the superintendent to pursue a one-time federal earmark to build a district-wide instructional framework and offset an expected cut to Title One funding.
Members endorsed a letter to state legislators arguing Lunenburg's Chapter 70 funding formula undercounts its per-pupil spending and excludes transportation costs.
The FY26 monthly budget report showed spending running ahead of the same point last year, with the electrical and legal lines over budget.

why_it_matters: The bus fee stays in place for families who use it, separate from and regardless of the outcome of the townwide override vote in May.
Ending the lifelong learning program removes a district-run adult offering, though students already enrolled will finish the current session before it closes.
The letter to legislators is an ask, not a change in funding -- any shift in how Chapter 70 treats transportation or per-pupil spending depends on action in Boston, not this committee.

ours.headline: Committee voted to keep charging the student bus fee despite members calling it unfair, citing budget desperation.

watch_next: May town meeting and ballot vote on the two-tier FY27 override
The stormwater task force's meeting the following day on a possible separate stormwater article

what_happened.line: The Select Board, Finance Committee and School Committee voted unanimously to pursue a two-tier FY27 override rather than a single override number.
The boards pulled stormwater out of the tier-two override and chose not to bring a standalone stormwater override article this cycle, deferring to the stormwater task force.
The School Committee raised its lower-tier override ask to restore fifth-grade band, leaving the higher tier unchanged.
Officials said they could not guarantee the higher override tier would avoid another override request next year, citing volatile costs like health insurance.
The boards agreed to bring in a paid communications professional to help plan joint messaging for town meeting and the ballot.

why_it_matters: A two-tier override means voters may face a choice between two different tax-bill impacts rather than one number, decided at May town meeting and on the ballot.
The lower tier's dollar figure now includes restoring fifth-grade band, and stormwater funding was pulled out of the override question entirely for now.
The boards themselves said the top tier is not guaranteed to be the last override ask, which residents should weigh alongside whatever figures appear in town-meeting materials.

ours.headline: TriBoard formally voted to pursue a two-tier (not single-number) FY27 override, dropping stormwater from it

watch_next: The tri-board override meeting the following night
The override vote at town meeting and the town election

what_happened.line: The committee voted to ask town meeting for only its lowest override tier, not a higher amount.
It voted to accept a reduced fallback budget for use if that override fails.

The fallback adds an English learner teacher, restored assistant principals, and a special education position, while cutting athletic trainer hours, sports, transportation, custodial and technology lines.
Middle school sports stay cut even if the override passes, to keep the requested amount manageable.
The committee voted to stop paying this year's Massachusetts Association of School Committees dues.

why_it_matters: Residents will be asked to vote on this override at the tri-board meeting, town meeting and the town election; a no vote triggers the fallback cuts described above.
The fallback ties athletic and band transportation cuts to preserving staffing positions at the primary and Turkey Hill schools, a trade-off the committee named directly.
Class sizes and support staffing at the primary school depend on whether the assistant principal and special education positions are funded or cut.

ours.headline: School Committee locked in its override request; without it, elementary classes grow and sports/band busing are cut.

what_happened.line: Select Board authorized a license agreement and waived building-department fees to advance the Food Pantry's move to 30 School Street.
A resident disputed the building commissioner's call that the new structure counts as permanent rather than temporary.
Board publicly introduced incoming town manager Jessica "Jack" Miller.
Zoning cleanup and a stormwater fee-bylaw article were referred to the planning board for the November 17 special town meeting.
Board declined to pursue a MassWorks grant this cycle to study senior housing at the former TCP school, citing a need for more public discussion.

why_it_matters: The food pantry's site status and its permanent-vs-temporary classification affect what oversight and process apply to future town-building decisions.
The stormwater bylaw change would tie fee amounts to a planning-board schedule that can change without a town meeting vote, which residents will be asked to weigh in November.
Passing on the MassWorks grant this cycle means no funded study of TCP senior housing for now, leaving that option undecided.

ours.headline: Select Board advanced the Food Pantry's temporary move to 30 School Street, waiving fees and OK'ing a license.

what_happened.line: The Select Board voted to recommend a lower, net education-aid figure than the school committee requested for Thursday's special town meeting article.
The board voted to create a special revenue fund from Winter Recovery Assistance Program money to fund a citizen petition restoring cut middle school and some high school sports.
The board voted, unanimously and as amended, to send a letter to state legislative leaders supporting the voter-approved audit of the Massachusetts legislature.
The board approved a permit for the Eagle House supporters' fall fundraiser toll booth in town center.

why_it_matters: Thursday's special town meeting will ask voters to act on both the school aid article and the sports-restoration article the board discussed tonight, and the board's recommended aid figure differs from what the school committee asked for.
The sports article's funding source is one-time snow-and-ice relief money rather than a new line in the operating budget, which shapes what happens after this year if the article passes.
A resident's public comment tied a recent increase in state aid to whether the school budget should be treated as level-service, a question the board's article recommendation touches directly.

ours.headline: Select Board recommends a lower education-aid figure than the school committee for Thursday's special town meeting article.

what_happened.line: The Select Board ratified Jessica Jack Miller as assistant town manager, effective September 8.
The board held off deciding how to apply new state winter-storm relief funds against the FY26 snow-and-ice deficit, pending word from the School and Finance Committees.
The board granted the food pantry permission to use temporary trailers at 30 School Street once a use agreement is drafted.
The board set warrant open and close dates for a special town meeting on November 17, 2026.
The board declared a 1998 ambulance surplus and closed a utility pole petition hearing.

why_it_matters: The snow-and-ice deficit decision affects how a budget shortfall gets closed -- by a transfer, a reappropriation of state funds, or some mix -- with the amount still unconfirmed pending a state review.
The food pantry's move to temporary trailers affects a service residents rely on after its current site loses heat this winter.
The November special town meeting warrant will carry articles residents will be asked to vote on, including any snow-and-ice or state-aid items now under discussion.

ours.headline: Select Board ratified Jessica Jack Miller as assistant town manager, deferred snow-and-ice relief funds decision

what_happened.line: Select Board members, the facilities director, and the town's building design committee toured Brooks House and the former TCP school in person to assess condition.
A food pantry representative questioned whether Brooks House can hold the pantry, citing water, bathroom, and floor-load needs, with no alternative site ready by October 1st.
The tour covered TCP's boiler leaks, asbestos-related ceiling costs, and ADA-trigger cost thresholds on roof work, with several cost figures described as estimates still to be confirmed.
A board member asked what basis existed for a roof-cost figure presented at a 2023 special town meeting; the facilities director said no formal roofer estimate existed at that time.
No votes were taken on the properties; the meeting ended with a vote to adjourn.

why_it_matters: Any eventual decision on Brooks House or TCP — including where the food pantry operates — will carry repair, ADA-compliance, and asbestos-abatement costs that a future town meeting may be asked to fund.
Whether roof or renovation work crosses an ADA-trigger cost threshold changes the scope and cost of any project at TCP, which affects what gets proposed to voters.
The pantry's relocation options remain unresolved, which matters to anyone who relies on that service or lives near either building.

ours.headline: Select Board and design committee toured Brooks House and TCP in person to assess building condition ahead of a future decision on the properties.

what_happened.line: The Select Board approved the September 3 special town meeting warrant, including three articles on the FY27 school budget shortfall and restoring middle school athletics and transportation.
The board voted unanimously to add the school committee's own shortfall article to that warrant.

The town manager said no certified free cash exists yet for the citizen petition seeking a free cash transfer, and town counsel is still reviewing which fund types the article's available funds language can legally draw from.
The next Select Board meeting is set for September 1, likely including warrant petitioners presenting their articles ahead of the September 3 vote.

why_it_matters: Residents will be asked at the September 3 special town meeting to vote on additional money for the FY27 school operating budget and on restoring middle school sports and student-athlete transportation.
One of the three articles names a funding source, certified free cash or available funds, that town officials say is not yet certified and may not be confirmed as usable before the vote.
Two of the three articles address the same school shortfall and were left unresolved as written, so town meeting itself may need to sort out overlap between them.

The board ratified a new principal assessor and part-time principal clerk and appointed a new Green Communities associate member.
A tour of TC Pacios and Brooks House with the Municipal Building Design Committee was scheduled for August 11th.

why_it_matters: The direction on TC Pacios starts the process toward a future town meeting vote on repairing or tearing down the building, which will carry a capital cost either way.
The rejected sewer bids mean the 100 Laura Lane connection will take a mixed in-house/vendor approach, which can affect its cost and schedule.
Residents watching the September 3rd special town meeting warrant should note that a free-cash-funded athletics article, if brought forward, cannot legally be voted on that date.

what_happened.line: Select Board and the building design committee leaned toward demolishing TC Pacios rather than repairing it, with no formal vote taken.
The Facilities Director was tasked with cost estimates for either a roof replacement or asbestos abatement plus full demolition, to feed the FY28 capital plan.
A roof-repair fund had been double-appropriated after a 2023 transfer was never reflected in MUNIS; town meeting corrected it this past May.
Election voting equipment and polling are being permanently moved out of TC Pacios to the schools, with a mobile trailer for storage.
The committee was asked to bring formal recommendations on both TC Pacios and Brooks House to a future meeting; its next meeting is August 3rd.

why_it_matters: Whether TC Pacios is repaired or demolished will shape the FY28 capital plan and what residents are asked to fund next.
The building's boiler failed a required state inspection and needs repair within 30 days or the town faces state fines, a cost pressure independent of the long-term decision.
Moving the polling location and election storage out of TC Pacios changes where some residents vote.

ours.headline: Select Board leaned toward demolishing TC Pacios rather than repairing it, pending a formal committee vote.

what_happened.line: The Select Board voted unanimously to call a citizen-petition special town meeting for September 3, 2026, opening the warrant July 28 and closing it August 7.
The board is still working to line up a stand-in moderator for that night, since town moderator Tim Murphy told the board he is unavailable September 3.
The board approved the warrant for the September 1 state primary election.
The board ratified the DPW collective bargaining agreement with Teamsters Local 170, following an earlier executive-session vote.
The board chose to keep running the special town meeting's legal ad in the weekly Ledger rather than switch to the daily Sentinel.

why_it_matters: The September 3 special town meeting is where residents act on the citizen petition's warrant article, and the schedule set here fixes the deadlines for that vote.
Who presides as moderator affects how that meeting is run, and the board is still confirming a deputy or temporary moderator can serve.
The ratified DPW union contract sets pay and working terms that flow into future town budgets.

ours.headline: The Select Board called a citizen-petition special town meeting for September 3, setting the warrant and hearing schedule.

what_happened.line: The select board heard the school committee's request for a warrant article adding state aid to the FY27 school budget but took no vote on it.
A citizens' petition has forced an earlier special town meeting than the board had planned.
The board's own figure for the net increase in education aid, after assessments, is still pending Finance Committee review.
The board approved the 2026 special town election warrant unanimously.
The board approved an Eagle Scout loafing shed project at the DPW yard and appointed Richard Howard to the Trust Fund Commission.

why_it_matters: Residents will eventually be asked to vote at a special town meeting on an article appropriating additional state aid to the school operating budget, though the select board has not yet voted on placing it and the exact amount is still being worked out.

The spending plan behind that request changed between the school committee's July 8 and July 15 meetings, and any warrant article involving money still requires a Finance Committee hearing before it goes to voters.
The petition changes the town meeting's timing, so the date itself — set to be discussed at a board meeting the following Monday — is something residents should track.

ours.headline: A citizens' petition forced an earlier special town meeting to consider added state aid for the school budget.

watch_next: A joint meeting between the Select Board and the Municipal Building Design Committee on TCP, planned for mid-to-late August 2026

what_happened.line: The board set a path toward deciding whether to demolish or renovate the deteriorating TCP building, asking the Municipal Building Design Committee for a formal recommendation to feed fall capital planning.
The board directed staff to draft its overdue, town-meeting-directed report on selling or long-term leasing the Brooks House, targeted for completion by the fall town meeting.

The Finance Committee and Select Board approved FY2026 year-end transfers, covering legal expenses, the sealer of weights and measures, and town report printing, drawn from a vacant planning board salary line.
The board voted to approve the Town Manager's proposed FY27 goals, including a review of outsourcing payroll processing and work toward adopting several tabled financial policies.

why_it_matters: Whichever way the TCP decision goes, the cost was described as able to consume most or all of a year's capital plan, which shapes what other town projects can be funded that year.
The Brooks House report determines the town's public path for a building it has been directed by town meeting to resolve, and residents may see options at a future town meeting.
Financial policies under discussion -- OPEB funding, reserves, and revenue projections -- bear on the town's long-term borrowing capacity and, eventually, the tax rate.

ours.headline: Select Board moves toward a decision on demolishing or renovating the deteriorating TCP building

what_happened.line: The board tabled ratification of the new DPW union contract after labor counsel flagged discrepancies to resolve.
The board voted to take a temporary easement at 890 Flatill Road by eminent domain to keep the bridge project moving.
A dispute over how the town processed Richard Howard's Trust Fund Commission application went unresolved, with the appointment pushed to a future agenda.
Approval of the August 8 special town election warrant was put off a week so town counsel can review new mailing-notice language.
The board also adopted the current IRS mileage rate, named a new detective and other appointees, and reviewed executive-session employment agreements for several town staff.

why_it_matters: A stalled union contract leaves DPW workers' pay and terms unresolved and keeps a labor cost decision open for the town.
The eminent domain action affects a specific property owner on Flatill Road and clears the way for a town bridge project residents depend on.
The election warrant delay and the mailing-notice review could affect how voters are notified ahead of the August 8 special town election.

ours.headline: The board took the Flatill Road bridge land by eminent domain and tabled the DPW union contract over legal disputes.

what_happened.line: The state told the Select Board electronic voting machines cannot be discontinued for the August 8 special election; they must be used.
The board ratified the Town Manager's full slate of annual town appointments by roll call, including the entire police department roster.
The board separately voted its own set of annual appointments, covering roles like Animal Control Officer and Parking Clerk.
A chief's recommendation to promote an officer to detective has not yet been taken up; that officer is listed as SRO in this round.

why_it_matters: Residents voting in the August 8 special election will use electronic voting machines, not a discontinued or alternate method, because the state ruled it mandatory.
The ratified appointments keep town officer and police department roles filled without a public vacancy or hiring process at this meeting.

ours.headline: Electronic voting machines can't be discontinued for the August special election — the state says they're mandatory.

what_happened.line: The board voted to send state legislators a letter urging preservation of the Foundation Budget Review Commission and higher school aid in the FY27 state budget.
The board decided to hold a standalone public hearing on a dangerous/nuisance dog complaint rather than close the matter on the investigative report alone.
The group searching for a temporary food pantry site coalesced around the former School Street school, contingent on the School Committee agreeing to move T-ball off that site.
The board adopted an updated environmentally preferable purchasing policy, which will only come back for a vote when the policy itself changes.
The finance director asked to push fiscal year-end transfers between departments to July, where they still need votes from both the Select Board and Finance Committee by July 15.

why_it_matters: State school aid funds a significant share of the school budget, so the legislature's decision on the Foundation Budget Review Commission and aid levels affects how much the town has to raise locally.
The dangerous dog complaint will now get a separate public hearing, giving residents and the parties involved a formal chance to be heard before any decision.
Year-end transfers move money between town departments to cover shortfalls and require sign-off from both the Select Board and Finance Committee before the July 15 deadline.

ours.headline: The board voted to press the state legislature to preserve the Foundation Budget Review Commission and boost school aid in the FY27 budget.

The Americans with Disabilities Committee is not expected to meet again until it has a member-at-large and a Select Board representative assigned, possibly not until August.
Vacancies remain on the Conservation Committee, Cultural Council, Historical Commission and PAC.

why_it_matters: Residents interested in serving on a town board now know which seats are filled and which -- Conservation, Cultural Council, Historical Commission, PAC -- are still open.
The Personnel Committee's reconstitution affects how the town handles personnel policy matters going forward.
A delay in staffing the Americans with Disabilities Committee could postpone its work on accessibility issues into the fall.

ours.headline: The Select Board reconstituted the Personnel Committee as a five-member body and filled its seats along with most other town board vacancies.

page.overview:
The Finance Committee is a committee of 7 members appointed for terms of 3 years, each so arranged that the terms of as nearly an equal number of members as is possible shall expire each year. The members are appointed by a committee consisting of 1 member of the Select Board chosen by the Select Board; 1 member of the School Committee chosen by the SC; and the Town Moderator.
The Finance Committee has the following duties, in accordance with the Town's Charter, Section 2-1(c):
The Finance Committee shall have the primary responsibility to report to the Town Meeting on the proposed budget of the Town Manager and all warrant articles having a fiscal impact on the Town, as more particularly detailed in the Charter, Town Bylaws, and the laws of the Commonwealth; before preparing its final recommendations, the Finance Committee shall hold 1 or more Public Hearings to permit public discussion on the subject matter of the articles contained in the warrant.
After the Town Manager has prepared the budget, the Finance Committee shall consult with the Town Manager and recommend any modifications it deems appropriate before the budget is filed with the Town Clerk.
The Finance Committee shall have all other powers conferred on finance committees by the General Laws.
For information on the Town's financial policies, please refer to the Select Board Policies and Procedures (PDF) on the Select Board Page.

watch_next: Select Board and School Committee action on the RAP fund and school choice offset for article three, expected the week following this meeting
The special town meeting vote on all three warrant articles

what_happened.line: Finance Committee unanimously recommended the school spending plan funded by new state aid, covering a second grade teacher, reading specialist, assistant principal, music teacher, and reduced athletic transportation costs.
The committee deferred the second warrant article to town meeting itself, since its own petitioner plans to move to pass it over.

The committee also deferred the third article, covering middle and high school sports funding, because its funding source had not yet been established by the Select Board or ratified by the School Committee.

Town officials informally agreed to apply a school choice credit to reduce the amount needed for the sports-funding article, pending action by the Select Board and School Committee the following week.

why_it_matters: Residents will be asked to vote on all three warrant articles at the special town meeting, including whether to fund the school positions and restored athletic transportation described in article one.

The mechanism behind article three -- a possible new special-purpose fund drawn from RAP money -- was still undecided at this meeting, so what residents vote on for sports funding may change before town meeting.

Town counsel advised that the article three motion will be worded more generally than the printed warrant article, since town meeting cannot legally earmark school-budget funds for a specific purpose.

ours.headline: Finance Committee recommended the new-state-aid school spending plan, but deferred the funding source for the rest of the warrant to town meeting itself.

watch_next: Select board meeting, August 18, on where WRAP snow-and-ice funds are directed
Finance Committee public hearing on the citizens petition, August 27

what_happened.line: A resident presented a cost model for a citizens petition to restore cut school sports and transportation ahead of the August 27 public hearing.
The chair asked the school committee to meet before that hearing, and the petitioner was directed to work out the funding mechanism with the town manager, select board, and town counsel.

Town counsel's opinion on what counts as "other available funds" for the article will be circulated, and the select board will decide August 18 whether new state snow-and-ice reimbursement money goes into a restricted fund or free cash.
The committee concluded the Finance Committee Reserve Fund likely cannot be used for the petition article, since the need appears foreseeable rather than an emergency.
The superintendent proposed directing any additional state aid toward literacy staffing and behavioral support rather than general class-size reduction, which drew extended debate.

why_it_matters: Town meeting will be asked to vote on the citizens petition article, and how it would be funded is not yet resolved.
Whether free cash, a state reimbursement fund, or the Reserve Fund can legally cover the article affects whether the article as written can proceed or needs to be scaled back on the floor.
How the district would spend any additional state aid -- staffing versus class size -- is now part of the same funding conversation.

ours.headline: The town is racing to fund a citizens petition restoring cut sports and transportation before the August 27 hearing.

watch_next: August 13 special town meeting presentation from the school committee, superintendent and petitioner Mandy Gilman
August 27 public hearing on the warrant article

what_happened.line: The Finance Committee heard the superintendent's plan to use FY27 state aid gains plus health insurance savings to fund five items, including two reading specialists, a full-time vice principal and tutoring seats.

An additional special town meeting is expected before September 3; a joint presentation from the school committee, superintendent and petitioner Mandy Gilman is set for August 13, with a public hearing on the article August 27.
The committee reorganized for the year, re-electing Chris Manard as chair and electing Peter Beardmore vice chair and Tom Gray clerk.
Department and school budget preview presentations, previously done jointly with the tri-board, will move to November or December, ahead of formal budget season.
The committee's capital planning committee seat was left unfilled and tabled for a future meeting.

why_it_matters: The staffing items the superintendent wants funded -- reading specialists, tutoring seats, a full-time vice principal and music teacher -- touch classrooms directly and are proposed to be paid from state aid and health insurance savings rather than new local tax dollars.
The special town meeting warrant article gets a public airing August 13 and a formal hearing August 27, which is where residents can weigh in before any vote.
Moving budget preview presentations earlier, to November/December, changes when residents can first see department and school budget details each cycle.

ours.headline: Finance Committee reorganized under new leadership and moved budget previews earlier ahead of a special town meeting

watch_next: A future Finance Committee meeting where year-end transfers and the fiscal policy list are actually taken up
Whether the chair, once back, moves the July reorg/vice-chair election date

what_happened.line: With the chair away, Finance Committee deferred year-end transfers to a future meeting rather than acting on them.
The committee compiled a list of fiscal policies to review later, including free cash, revenue projections, stabilization accounts and OPEB, without voting on any.
Members discussed reviving a joint committee with the Select Board and School Committee but reached no consensus, leaving it for the chair to take up on his return.
Election of a new vice chair was postponed until the chair is back, with the usual July date now in question for one member's availability.

why_it_matters: Year-end transfers move town money between budget lines after the fact, and residents will not see that reconciliation until a later meeting.
The stabilization-account policy under discussion touches when reserves such as the fire truck fund can be tapped versus held for one-time needs.
A revived tri-board committee would change how the Select Board, School Committee and Finance Committee coordinate on shared fiscal decisions.

ours.headline: Finance Committee, minus its chair, deferred nearly every substantive item — transfers, policy review, tri-board revival — to a future meeting.

watch_next: Next Finance Committee meeting, June 11
Whether the state Senate aid to Lunenburg is finalized and signed into law

what_happened.line: Finance Committee weighed reopening the FY27 school budget after new state Senate aid, but took no formal action, leaving the town-meeting-approved budget in place.
A member urged that any alternate budget proposal next year be vetted by the finance committee and tri-board before reaching town meeting.
Members debated revisiting reserve, free cash, and OPEB contribution policy given the tight budget year, without resolving the question.
The chair said any additional state aid, once finalized, would not be spent all at once and could instead be allocated at a special town meeting.
The committee set its next meeting for June 11th and agreed to resume work on the financial policies document ahead of FY28.

why_it_matters: Whether the FY27 school budget already approved at town meeting gets reopened affects how much of the new state aid reaches classrooms versus reserves.
A special town meeting could be called to allocate any finalized state aid, which would be a vote residents get to weigh in on.
Reserve, free cash, and OPEB funding levels shape how much cushion the town has for future budget years and how steep future tax asks could be.

ours.headline: Committee debated reopening FY27 school budget after new state Senate aid, but leaned toward not disturbing the town-meeting-approved budget

watch_next: May town meeting, where article L (FY27 budget) and article M (the two override tiers) go to a town-wide vote
Finance Committee meeting, April 23

what_happened.line: Finance Committee voted 4-2 to recommend both tiers of a Proposition 2½ override for town meeting.
The FY27 omnibus balanced budget was recommended on a split 4-1-1 vote after a member argued it under-documents two new positions.
The committee voted 4-2 to add the assistant town manager and HR director positions to the salary grid, which a member said bypassed the town's normal job-description process.
Several prior 5-0 and other warrant-article recommendations were re-voted so the chair's vote could be added before the warrant is finalized.
The next Finance Committee meeting was set for April 23, skipping April 9.

why_it_matters: Town meeting will vote on both override tiers as well as the underlying FY27 budget, so a resident's tax bill depends on which of these articles pass.
Adding the two new town-hall positions to the salary grid affects what those roles cost the town, and the committee's recommendation was split, not unanimous.
The re-votes and the finance committee's own annual report will accompany the warrant residents receive by mail before they vote.

ours.headline: Finance Committee voted to recommend both Prop 2½ override tiers for town meeting, 4-2 each

watch_next: The next Finance Committee meeting, when the full board is expected to take up the override recommendation.
A future vote on the FY27 omnibus town/school budget article, once closeout and transfer figures are final.

what_happened.line: The committee put off recommending a position on the FY27 Proposition 2½ override until the full five-member board can meet.
It also deferred the FY27 omnibus town and school operating budget because final transfer figures were not yet ready.
A new special-purpose health insurance stabilization fund transfer passed its recommendation on a 4-1 vote.
A proposed Assistant Town Manager/HR Director grade change was pushed to the next meeting after members said it needed further discussion.
Most routine warrant articles -- revolving funds, the FY27 capital budget, and the water and solid waste enterprise funds -- were recommended for approval.

why_it_matters: The override recommendation touches what residents are asked to approve at town meeting or the ballot, and the committee is not yet on record with a position.
The FY27 omnibus budget funds town and school operations for the coming year; its numbers were not final at this meeting.
The health insurance stabilization fund is a new savings mechanism for a cost that affects both town and school budgets, and it did not pass without dissent.

ours.headline: Finance Committee set warrant recommendations but held its override vote for the full board

watch_next: April 6 virtual Finance Committee meeting: vote on warrant articles and the committee's report
May 2 town meeting warrant vote and May 16 override ballot vote

what_happened.line: The Finance Committee closed its public hearing on the FY27 school and town budgets without voting on the budget, an override, or any warrant article.

The superintendent laid out a level-funded budget with cuts to teaching positions, music, and athletics, against two override scenarios that would restore and add staff across schools, police, fire, DPW, and the library.
Draft warrant articles, including the override article itself, were walked through but not voted on.
The committee scheduled an additional virtual meeting for April 6 to vote on the warrant articles and finalize its report before the town meeting deadline.

why_it_matters: Whether voters pass a tier-1 or tier-2 override in May decides whether class sizes rise and positions such as teachers, a custodian, and an occupational therapy assistant go unfilled.
The warrant articles still being drafted will set exactly what residents are asked to vote on at town meeting and on the override ballot.
Town departments including police, fire, DPW, and the library face the same level-funded-versus-override choice as the schools.

ours.headline: School and town budgets face deep cuts unless voters pass a tier-1 or tier-2 override in May

watch_next: Continued public hearing, March 26 at 7:00
School Committee's voted budget presentation to the Finance Committee

what_happened.line: The Finance Committee opened its budget public hearing and voted to continue it to March 26 at 7:00.
A member said town bylaw requires the School Committee to present the budget it actually voted, with an explanation of major changes, not just a single line item.
The committee said it has not yet received an updated budget snapshot from the Select Board's own budget workshop with the town manager.
Both the school and town sides are expected to bring a core-services budget and a separate restoration or override budget rather than one dollar figure.
A member said residents need to know what a 'no' vote on the override would actually cut, not just see a total.

why_it_matters: Residents will eventually be asked to vote on an override, and this hearing is where the town and school budgets that frame that choice get explained before town meeting.
The bylaw question about the School Committee presenting its full voted budget, not just a line item, affects how much detail the public sees before deciding.
A continued hearing means the public comment window on the budget stays open into late March rather than closing now.

ours.headline: Finance Committee opened its budget public hearing and immediately continued it to March 26.

watch_next: The rescheduled FY27 budget public hearing on March 26
The tri-board meeting on March 19 to resolve the one-override-vs-two-override question

what_happened.line: Finance Committee recapped a tri-board session where all members agreed an override belongs on the ballot, but remained split on whether it should be one amount or two.

DPW's proposed FY27 budget came in higher than prior years, restoring pavement management funding the town manager's preliminary budget had cut, though one committee member said they will not support that restoration.
The town manager's office is being restructured: the communications and IT director position would be eliminated and a new assistant town manager position funded starting July 1.

The committee recommended moving a warrant article seeking money to legally investigate several neglected municipal trust funds from the annual town meeting to a special town meeting, so a firmer cost estimate can be developed first.
The FY27 budget public hearing was pushed back one week to March 26, with a tri-board meeting taking the committee's March 19 slot instead.

why_it_matters: An override, once the ballot format is settled, would raise property taxes for residents and the one-question-versus-two split changes how they vote on it.
The DPW budget still has to be finalized, and whether pavement management funding is restored affects road paving work and how storm water permit compliance gets funded.
The town manager's office restructuring changes which staff position handles human resources and IT/communications duties going forward.

ours.headline: Finance Committee reviewed FY27 department budgets amid a large town-school funding gap, with an override now expected.

watch_next: Tri-board meeting on the FY27 budget and override, March 10, 7:30pm, Town Hall (or Zoom)
PAC's promised breakdown of staff time between government and public-channel programming

what_happened.line: Finance Committee members leaned toward asking voters for a trimmed, level-service Proposition 2½ override rather than bundling town requests with the school committee's larger 'restoration' budget.
The concern was explicit: a 2012 override bundled similarly and failed by roughly two-to-one, leading to a decade of cuts.
The override's shape now goes to a tri-board meeting of town and school officials on March 10.

Public Access Cable described a widening deficit from falling Comcast franchise fees and a forced studio move, and agreed to start tracking how its staff time splits between government and public-channel work.
The Council on Aging presented a level-funded budget and the Library a modest increase, with a member asking the library to itemize all funding sources next time.

why_it_matters: Whether the town bundles a school 'restoration' ask into one override question or asks for less, level-service money affects every taxpayer's ballot choice and, town officials warned, whether any of it passes at all.
Public Access Cable's declining franchise-fee revenue and relocation could affect coverage of town and school meetings if the town doesn't take up funding it.
The library's state certification and state aid depend on the town meeting a minimum appropriation threshold, which this budget cycle sets.

ours.headline: Finance Committee warns a large school 'restoration' override could fail, as one did in 2012.

The Agricultural Commission shall have the primary responsibility of assisting in maintaining agriculture in Lunenburg. The Commission shall administer the Right to Farm Bylaw and will hold additional responsibilities as charged by the Board of Selectmen. The Commission is a component of the state's "Sustainable Development" program, thereby helping Lunenburg become eligible for various state grant programs. The Agricultural Commission can oversee, operate or run a Farmers' Market.
The Agricultural Commission shall develop a work plan to guide its activities. Such activities may include but are not limited to, the following: encouraging the continued pursuit of agriculture in Lunenburg; promoting agricultural-based economic opportunities in Town; mediating, advocating, educating, and/or negotiating on farming issues; working for the preservation of prime agricultural lands; and pursuing all initiatives appropriate to retaining farming in Lunenburg.
"Encouraging the continued pursuit of agriculture; promoting agriculturally based economic opportunities in town; mediating, advocating, educating and/or negotiating on farming issues; working for the preservation of prime agricultural lands; and pursuing all initiatives appropriate to retaining farming in Lunenburg."
The Agricultural Commission consists of five members and two alternate members appointed by the Board of Selectmen for terms of three years each. A majority of the membership shall be substantially engaged in the pursuit of agriculture. A vacancy occurring otherwise than by expiration of a term shall be filled for the unexpired term in the same manner as the original appointment.
Anyone and everyone interested in farming, pursuing farming, or seeking to help preserve, protect, and promote Lunenburg's agricultural heritage is always welcome.

Welcome to the website for the Lunenburg Architectural Preservation District Commission.
The 2015 Lunenburg Town Meeting established the Architectural Preservation District ("District") Bylaw ("Bylaw") to regulate the construction, demolition, or renovation of existing "Contributing Property" structures as defined by the bylaw within an established bounded District ("District"). The Bylaw was introduced at Town Meeting along with the Village District Bylaw, which created an overlay zoning district to encourage mixed-use commercial and residential development. While the Village District Bylaw encourages the economic vitalization of downtown Lunenburg, the Architectural Preservation District Bylaw ensures that it will not come at the expense of the town's historical character and integrity.
The Bylaw also mandated the creation of Design Guidelines ("Guidelines") to assist the Architectural Preservation District Commission ("APDC") in evaluating requests for construction, renovation, and demolition of structures that are 75 years old or older within the District, as shown in the District Map (PDF).
The Select Board shall appoint a five-member APDC to oversee the APD pursuant to this bylaw. Initially, two members shall be appointed for one year, two for two years, and one for three years; each successive appointment shall be made for three years. The Select Board may also appoint up to two alternate members, initially for terms of one, two, and three years, and for three-year terms thereafter.
To the extent achievable, the APDC shall be comprised of the following persons: a member of the Lunenburg Historical Commission; a design professional; a craftsperson or building contractor familiar with historic restoration; one resident of the APD, and one resident at large. Members and alternates of the APDC shall by reason of experience and/or education have demonstrable knowledge, interest, and ability to effectively carry out the APDC's responsibilities.
To request additional information or to inquire about a non-binding Administrative Review, please email Email APDC.

In Massachusetts, Assessors are either appointed or elected to three-year terms. The Assessors' primary responsibility is to value all real estate and personal property subject to taxation. Assessed valuations are based on "full and fair cash value" of as of the January 1st preceding each fiscal year. Ex. For Fiscal Year 2021, the assessment date is January 1, 2020, and market sales utilized for valuation purposes are from calendar year 2019. 
In order to maintain assessment at or near market value, the Assessors regularly compare property valuations with the selling prices of properties that have sold. Assessment-to-sale ration statistics are analyzed to determine the median assessment level, as well as assessment uniformity. No valuation methodology can accurately predict what a property will sell for. 
Under the umbrella of Massachusetts state and local town laws, Lunenburg’s Assessing organization will work with the town operations and our citizens to meet our vision for delivering a fair and equitable taxation for our citizens. The Lunenburg Board of Assessors will evolve and administer a service of “Best Practices” methodologies consistent with our Vision. These practices will ensure equitable treatment and compassion for all our citizens.
The Board of Assessors has empowered an Assessor organization that has the capability to evaluate and assess all property at its full and fair market value. This is accomplished through a rigorous measurement of property, collection of appropriate data, analysis and maintenance of all property tax data records. Additionally, the Assessor department administers a motor vehicle excise tax, real estate and motor vehicle tax abatements, and all statutory tax exemptions as allowed by law. The Assessor Organization will work cohesively with other town departments.
The Fiscal Year 2026 tax rate is $14.39 per thousand. 
Vision Statement
To provide Lunenburg with fiscal stability; by promptly, fairly and equitably determining the valuation of all real and personal property located within the geographic boundaries of Lunenburg; and execute the Assessor functions as described by Mass General Laws, the Mass Department of Revenue and the Citizens of Lunenburg. 
This will be accomplished through a rigorous measurement of property, collection appropriate data, analysis and maintenance of all property tax data records. Additionally, the Assessor department will also administer a motor vehicle excise tax, real, tax abatements, and all statutory tax exemptions as allowed by law. The Assessor Organization will work cohesively with other town departments.
The Lunenburg Board of Assessors will actively reach out to the citizens of Lunenburg, to assure all members of the community are aware of all taxation practices and exemptions available. The assessors will assist with clarification these practices & exemptions, as well as guide citizens in their usage of these exemptions.
Mission Statement
Under the umbrella of Massachusetts state and local town laws; Lunenburg's Assessor organization will work with the town operations and our citizens to meet our vision for delivering a fair and equitable taxation for our citizens
The Lunenburg Board of Assessors will evolve and administer a series of “Best Practices” methodologies consistent our Vision. These practices will assure equitable treatment and compassion for all our citizens.
Board of Directors will empower an Assessor organization that will have the capability to evaluate and assess all property at its full and fair market value, for the purpose of fair and equitable taxation.
This will be accomplished through a rigorous measurement of property, collection appropriate data, analysis and maintenance of all property tax data records. Additionally, the Assessor department will also administer a motor vehicle excise tax, real, tax abatements, and all statutory tax exemptions as allowed by law. The Assessor Organization will work cohesively with other town departments.
The Lunenburg BOA activities are defined within our Town Charter.
As members of the Lunenburg Board of Assessors, (Both elected and appointed), we are in fact employees of the Town of Lunenburg, and subject to all Mass Conflict of Interest Laws and regulations: G.L c 268A.

Section 1: General
The Budget Task Force shall be charged with recommending scenarios for a three to five-year sustainable fiscal plan for the Town of Lunenburg. A sustainable fiscal plan is defined as a financial forecast that uses realistic assumptions for revenue and expenditure growth that allow the Town to provide services that meet residents’ expectations and meet ongoing expenditure obligations through regularly occurring revenues. Said fiscal plan shall consider, as an example, alternative revenue sources; overrides and exclusions under proposition 2 ½; cuts in service; contracting out of services, as well as other measures. Said fiscal plan shall include both operational and capital budgets for the town. The Budget Task Force shall consult with pertinent departments as it formulates its plan.
The Budget Task Force shall present its findings and recommendations to the Select Board, Finance Committee, and School Committee no later than December 31, 2024.
Section 2: Tasks and Responsibilities
Collect data on revenue and expenditure historical trends, and project future estimates based on trends and various assumptions.
Benchmark municipal and school performance, programs, expenditures, and revenues with comparable municipalities.
Examine potential revenue sources; overrides and exclusions under Proposition 2 ½ as well as non-tax and non-override revenue sources in compliance with the Town Financial Policy including costs, feasibility, potential savings, and other impacts of potential adoption and implementation; cuts in service; contracting out of services, as well as other measures.
Evaluate strategies to properly staff municipal and school operations while managing growth of personnel costs.
Analyze capital project funding needs and impacts, including long term large capital projects.
Include both operational and capital budgets in the fiscal plan recommendations.
Assess the impact any increased taxes and fees will have on taxpayers and residents, including the tax impact of debt exclusions related to large capital projects under consideration.
Section 3: Membership and Meetings
 The Select Board does hereby establish the Budget Task Force as a temporary working group consisting of seven (7) members:Select Board, 1 representative and an optional alternate appointed by it
School Committee, 1 representative and an optional alternate appointed by it
Finance Committee, 1 representative and an optional alternate appointed by it
Town Manager
School Superintendent
Town Finance Director
School Director of Administration and Finance
The Select Board shall reserve the right to continue the Budget Task Force after its task is complete in order to adjust the plan due to changing circumstances.
The Budget Task Force shall meet at a time and place mutually agreeable to its membership. 
Voting Power: All duly appointed members shall have full voting power.
A quorum shall consist of four (4) members.\
The election of officers including a Chair, Vice-Chair, and Clerk shall be by a majority vote of the Budget Task Force.
The recording of minutes and votes of all meetings as prescribed by Open Meeting Law. Copies of the minutes shall be submitted to the Town Clerk as prescribed in the Town Bylaws and according to Open Meeting Law.
This charge was adopted by the Lunenburg Select Board at their June 18, 2024 meeting and may be amended at any future meeting.

The goal of the Capital Planning Committee is to provide a means of planning for necessary expenditures for maintenance, equipment, and/ or improvements of the capital assets and infrastructure of the Town of Lunenburg.
The Capital Planning Committee shall research, study and advise the Selectmen and Finance Committee of the requests for short and long-range capital purchases for the Town. The Committee shall be charged with facilitating the coordination between community objectives, capital needs, and fiscal capacity. The Committee will help the Town to understand the tax impact of the capital expenditures and consider the relative need, timing, and cost of each capital expenditure. The Committee shall consider all written requests and make recommendations. The Committee shall provide a written report to assist the Selectmen and Finance Committee in keeping the community informed about the Town's future anticipated needs and projects that will be voted on at the Annual Town Meeting.
The Capital Planning Committee receives its authorization from Article 27 of the Town's Bylaws which states, "There shall be a Capital Planning Committee. That Committee shall consist of five members to be appointed as follows: One member each designated by the Financial Committee, the Select Board, the School Committee, and the Planning Board, and a fifth member chosen at large by the Town Moderator. Each member shall be appointed for a term of three years, said terms staggered so that nearly an equal number of members shall be appointed each year. The Capital Planning Committee shall establish and update a comprehensive capital plan.
The committee shall at least annually provide its materials to the Chief Administrative and Financial Officer so that the Chief Administrative and Financial Officer will meet the obligations of the Office set forth in Section 6-6 (sic) of the Lunenburg Town Charter. The Capital Planning Committee shall be responsible for providing a complete inventory of town property, real and personal, including school property, in conjunction with the Chief Administrative and Financial Officer. (ATM 5/05/07, Art.21)

The Cemetery Commission is an elected three-member Commission with terms of three years each. The board of cemetery commissioners have the responsibility to make regulations governing the care, superintendence, and management of all public burial grounds in Lunenburg and to lay out existing public burial grounds and may lot out in lots or other suitable subdivision with proper paths, lanes, and ways appropriate for burial use any other land acquired by the town for burial purposes. The day-to-day care and maintenance of the cemeteries shall be under the supervision of the Town Manager, which has been delegated to the DPW Director as the Cemetery is a division under the Department of Public Works.
Lunenburg has two major cemeteries:
North Cemetery is located on Holman Street at the corner of Highland Street
South Cemetery is located on Page Street off Lancaster Avenue

The Lunenburg Cultural Council is responsible for disbursing funds received from the Massachusetts Cultural Council for local cultural and artistic activities.
The mission of the Lunenburg Cultural Council is to nurture and promote a diverse range of artistic and cultural programs for the benefit of Lunenburg and surrounding communities.
We accomplish this through the annual allocation of state grants for local projects and by producing cultural events using locally-raised funds.
The Council reviews proposals and grants funds to local applicants for a variety of projects that benefit Lunenburg citizens. Local Cultural Councils support community-based projects in the arts, sciences, and humanities every year. The state legislature provides an annual appropriation to the Massachusetts Cultural Council, a state agency, which then allocates funds to each community.
The Lunenburg Cultural Council recognizes that the arts, humanities, and interpretive sciences form an important part of Lunenburg's history, identity, and vision. We are committed to nurturing our artistic community through supporting events that are accessible, collaborative, and fun for Lunenburg residents and visitors of all ages.

Section 1: General
The Lunenburg Economic Development Committee is being formed by the Planning Board in order to better assist, counsel, and advise the residents of Lunenburg, the Planning Board, other Town Boards and Departments, and Lunenburg businesses on ways to promote the local economy.
Section 2: Functions
Mission: The Lunenburg Economic Development Committee is committed to promoting business development that will enhance the character, culture, and commerce in Lunenburg. The Committee shall investigate current economic conditions to provide advice to Town Departments on economic development policy; meet and work with current Lunenburg businesses and prospective businesses; coordinate its activities with the appropriate Town Boards and Commissions; and work cooperatively with businesses and state agencies to retain, develop and promote businesses in Lunenburg.
Section 3: Membership & Meetings
The Committee shall be composed of five regular members serving three-year terms appointed by the Planning Board as follows: One member recommended by the Agricultural Commission that owns a business in Lunenburg and shall initially be appointed for a three-year term; One member recommended by the Open Space Committee and shall initially be appointed for a three-year term; One member recommended by the Conservation Commission and shall initially be appointed for a two-year term; Two members that are residents of Lunenburg, one shall initially be appointed for a two-year term and one shall initially be appointed for a one year term. In addition to the regular members, there will be four ex-officio members as follows: One member of the Select Board chosen annually by the Select Board; One member of the Planning Board chosen annually by the Planning Board; The Director of Planning and Economic Development; and A Lunenburg Business Owner.
After the initial term, all members shall serve a three-year term.
Voting Power: All duly appointed members shall have full voting power; ex-officio members shall not have the power to vote.
Resignation: Members of the Committee shall notify the Chairman of the Committee and the Planning Board of their resignation.
Vacancies: Any vacancies shall be filled in the same manner as the original appointment.
The election of officers including at least a Chairman, Vice-Chairman, and Clerk and shall be elected annually by a majority vote of the Committee.
A quorum shall consist of three members.
The Committee shall keep a recording of minutes and votes of all meetings as prescribed by the Open Meeting Law. This charge may be amended at any time.

Section 1: General
The Lunenburg Green Communities Committee will work with the Massachusetts Department of Energy Resources to learn of grant opportunities for energy conservation and renewable energy generation and will apply for appropriate grants. The Committee will ensure the Town retains its status as a designated Green Community.
Section 2: Functions
Mission: The Lunenburg Green Communities Committee will focus on improving and promoting energy efficiency in town and school facilities, infrastructure, and vehicles. The Committee will help raise awareness, educate, advise, and motivate the Town of Lunenburg residents and businesses to reduce waste, reduce energy use, conserve resources, reduce emissions/carbon footprint, and embrace clean and renewable energy options.
Responsibilities
Identify and develop grant submissions for Green Communities Competitive Grant annually that corresponds with the mission of this committee and is consistent with the Town's goals;
Develop action steps to ensure Lunenburg remains designated as a Department of Energy Resources Green Community;
Facilitate town participation in DOER programs, grants, and incentives;
Serve as an information resource for town residents and business owners on the benefits of energy and resource conservation;
Increase constituents' awareness of and promote resource conservation methods, energy efficiency programs, utility rebates, and state/federal programs to promote energy efficiency, waste reduction, recycling, and overall enhancements to long-term sustainability and resilience in response to environmental, resource, and energy challenges;
Report at least once annually on its activities to the Select Board.
Section 3: Membership & Meetings
The Committee shall be composed of 5 regular members serving three-year terms appointed by the Select Board and two associate members. Two members shall initially be appointed to a three-year term, two members shall initially be appointed to a two-year term, and one member shall initially be appointed to a one-year term. After the initial term, all regular members shall serve a three-year term. The associate members shall be appointed to a three-year term.
In addition to the regular members, the Committee shall consult with the Town Manager, the town departments that oversee the facilities and energy accounts, the School Superintendent, and the School Facilities Director that oversees the school facilities and school energy accounts in order to ascertain future energy projects, areas where energy savings are needed, and replacement schedule for vehicles.
Voting Power: All duly appointed regular members shall have full voting power.
Resignation: Members of the Committee shall notify the Chairman of the Committee, the Town Manager, and the Select Board of their resignation.
